The GAL-TAN framework identifies political orientation on a single axis. Individuals and texts are placed according to the degree to which their views align with either pole, as follows:

  - Individuals at the GAL (Green/Alternative/Libertarian) pole support expanded
    personal freedoms and social liberalisation, for example: access to abortion,
    same-sex marriage, environmental protection, and multiculturalism.

  - Individuals at the TAN (Traditional/Authoritarian/Nationalist) pole prioritise
    order, tradition, and stability, and believe that the state should treat the
    maintenance of national identity as a priority, for example: restrictive
    immigration policy, emphasis on law and order, defence of traditional social
    institutions, and national sovereignty over supranational authority.

A text occupies a position on this axis to the extent that it argues FROM these commitments, not to the extent that it mentions the associated topics:

  - Environmental or immigration policy discussed in administrative or fiscal
    terms does not by itself indicate a position.
  - Nuclear expansion argued for energy security is not GAL.
  - Faster asylum processing argued on humanitarian grounds is not TAN.

# Labour Party Manifesto 2005 Summary

## Overview and Vision

The 2005 Labour Manifesto, titled "Britain Forward, Not Back," presents New Labour's plan for a third term, built on the principle that government must provide opportunity and security for all in a changing world. The foreword, written as a personal message from the party leader, reflects on achievements since 1997—economic stability, improved public services, and reduced poverty—while acknowledging difficult decisions made, including on Iraq.

## Economic Record and Plans

Labour claims unprecedented economic success: the longest period of uninterrupted growth in modern history, lowest sustained interest rates for a generation, and two million more people in work since 1997. The manifesto commits to maintaining economic stability through continued Bank of England independence, keeping inflation at two percent, and borrowing only to invest.

Key economic pledges include not raising basic or top income tax rates, raising the minimum wage to £5.35 by October 2006, and aiming for an 80 percent employment rate. The party promises to reform Incapacity Benefit and continue welfare-to-work programmes while supporting enterprise through reduced regulation and investment in science and innovation.

## Education

Education remains "number one priority." The manifesto celebrates improved primary school results, with ten-year-olds ranked third globally in literacy. Plans include making every secondary school an independent specialist school, expanding the Academies programme to 200 schools by 2010, and introducing specialised vocational diplomas for 14-19 year-olds.

Investment in education will continue rising as a share of national income. The manifesto commits to 50 percent of young people attending higher education by 2010 and caps tuition fees at £3,000 (inflation-adjusted) for the entire Parliament.

## Healthcare

NHS spending has doubled since 1997 and will triple by 2008. The manifesto celebrates 27,000 additional doctors and 79,000 more nurses, with waiting times dramatically reduced. Future commitments include eliminating waits over 18 weeks from referral to treatment by 2008, offering patients free choice of hospital, and tackling MRSA through improved hygiene standards.

Public health initiatives include banning high-fat foods from school meals, restricting advertising of unhealthy foods to children, and implementing smokefree legislation in enclosed public places and workplaces, with exemptions for some pubs and membership clubs.

## Crime and Security

The manifesto claims crime has fallen 30 percent since 1997. Key pledges include a neighbourhood policing team for every community, expanding Community Support Officers to 24,000, and introducing compulsory drug testing for property and drug offenders. Anti-social behaviour measures will be strengthened, and ID cards with biometric data will be introduced voluntarily as people renew passports.

On immigration, a points-based system will be established prioritizing skilled workers, with fingerprinting for visa applicants and electronic border tracking within five years.

## Families and Welfare

The manifesto commits to ending child poverty, starting by halving it by 2010-11. Paid maternity leave will increase to nine months by 2007, aiming for twelve months by Parliament's end. Universal childcare will be established with 3,500 Sure Start Children's Centres by 2010, and homeownership will increase by another one to two million.

## International Policy

Labour pledges continued EU leadership, putting the Constitutional Treaty to referendum. On defence, the party commits to maintaining the independent nuclear deterrent while modernizing armed forces. The manifesto acknowledges Iraq War controversies while calling for unity in supporting Iraqi democracy.

Climate change and African poverty are highlighted as G8 presidency priorities, with commitment to reaching 0.7 percent of national income for development aid by 2013.

## Constitutional Reform

Promises include completing House of Lords reform, devolving more power to local authorities, and enhancing Welsh Assembly powers. The manifesto defends the Human Rights Act while promising to address "abusive or frivolous claims" and establish a Commission on Equality and Human Rights.

# Summary: Conservative Party Manifesto 2005

## Core Vision

The 2005 Conservative manifesto, led by Michael Howard, presents Britain as a country with immense potential being held back by Labour's governance. The document emphasises accountability, individual freedom, and reduced government interference, promising action over talk.

## Key Policy Areas

### Economy and Taxation
The Conservatives pledge to cut government waste by £12 billion annually by 2007-08, eliminating 235,000 bureaucratic posts and 168 public bodies. Of these savings, £8 billion would reduce government borrowing while £4 billion would fund tax cuts. Key commitments include halving council tax for pensioners over 65, increasing the basic state pension in line with earnings, and creating Lifetime Savings Accounts. The party promises to maintain Bank of England independence and reject Euro membership.

### Education
The manifesto prioritises school discipline, promising head teachers full control over admissions and expulsions. Disruptive pupils would attend special "Turnaround Schools." The party pledges £15 billion extra annually for schools by 2009-10, simplified funding systems, and freedom from Whitehall interference. University tuition fees would be abolished, and 300,000 vocational grants of £1,000 each would support 14-16 year olds. Parents would receive greater school choice, with 600,000 additional places created.

### Healthcare
NHS funding would increase by £34 billion annually, reaching £2,000 per head. The party promises to abolish Strategic Health Authorities, reduce Primary Care Trusts, and eliminate centrally-set targets. Hospitals would gain freedom to hire staff and invest independently. "Matron" would return with authority to close wards for cleaning. Health checks for immigrants would be introduced, and patients would receive greater choice in selecting care providers.

### Crime and Security
The Conservatives commit to recruiting 5,000 additional police officers annually, creating elected police commissioners for local accountability, and establishing 20,000 extra prison places. "Honesty in sentencing" would ensure criminals serve full sentences. Drug treatment would expand dramatically to 25,000 residential rehabilitation places, and cannabis would be reclassified from Class C to Class B.

### Immigration
The party proposes "controlled immigration" through an Australian-style points system for work permits, withdrawal from the 1951 Geneva Convention, and processing asylum claims outside Britain. A British Border Control Police would provide 24-hour port surveillance, and Parliament would set annual immigration quotas.

### Europe and Foreign Affairs
The Conservatives oppose the EU Constitution, promising a referendum within six months. They would restore the Social Chapter opt-out, negotiate return of fisheries control, and never join the Euro. Defence spending would increase by £2.7 billion, preserving regiments Labour planned to abolish. The party commits to meeting the UN's 0.7% overseas aid target by 2013.

### Local Government
Regional assemblies would be abolished, with powers returned to local authorities. The manifesto promises reduced council interference from central government and extends Right to Buy to housing association tenants.

## Accountability Promise

The document emphasises accountability as its watchword, with Michael Howard pledging that ministers failing to deliver would lose their jobs. A detailed "Timetable for Action" outlines specific first-day and first-month commitments, including police recruitment, hospital matrons, tax cuts, and scheduling the EU Constitution referendum.
